title: Teaching the Limited Capacity Brain: A Visual Guide and Model nd-model/
author: Mike Hobbiss
summary: Mike Hobbiss synthesises two conference talks into a visual model of teaching designed around the brain's genuinely limited capacity for attention and working memory - a limitation, he clarifies, that applies to everyone, not just struggling students. He walks through attention as a hard bottleneck to higher-order cognition (if task-relevant information doesn't fill it, irrelevant stimuli automatically will), and working memory as a second, downstream limited-capacity system that can typically hold only around four chunks of complex information at once. His central practical claim is that neither system's raw capacity can be meaningfully increased through training, so the only real lever available to teachers is filling both systems with the right information - primarily by reducing classroom distractions and by actively cueing attention toward what matters. Hobbiss's most generative idea is the 'cheat' available via long-term memory: information that is meaningfully connected in long-term memory can be recalled into working memory as a single chunk, dramatically expanding effective working-memory capacity - but only if that information has sufficient retrieval strength, which requires teachers to provide retrieval opportunities in advance of when students will actually need the knowledge, creating a virtuous cycle between working memory and long-term memory.
points: Hobbiss's foundational claim: attention functions as a hard bottleneck to all higher-order cognition - if task-relevant information doesn't fill a student's limited attentional capacity, irrelevant stimuli will automatically fill it instead.

His key working-memory statistic: working memory capacity is typically 'filled' by roughly four chunks of information when the material is relatively complex - a hard ceiling that cannot be meaningfully increased through training.

Since raw capacity cannot be trained up, Hobbiss argues the only real teaching lever is filling limited attention and working memory with the right information - primarily by reducing classroom distractions and actively cueing what's important.

His central 'cheat': information meaningfully connected in long-term memory can be recalled into working memory as a single chunk, dramatically expanding the effective amount of information a student can manipulate at once.

The catch: this only works if retrieval strength is high enough for the information to actually be recalled, meaning teachers must provide retrieval opportunities in advance of when students will need the knowledge - creating a virtuous cycle between working memory and long-term memory.
quotes: It is hopefully not too controversial a statement to say that attention and working memory are limited in capacity (and in their duration too, for that matter).
The important thing to take from all this though is that attention is a complete bottleneck to higher order processing, the gateway to complex cognition.
Unfortunately, increasing capacity (i.e. training) doesn't really seem to work for either attention or working memory.
This gives us our first key teaching message. That we need to do out best to reduce distractions in the classroom wherever possible.
Even more importantly in terms of overcoming capacity limitations, information which is meaningfully connected in long term memory can be recalled into working memory as a single 'chunk'.
This means that as teachers we need to ideally provide students with retrieval opportunities (which will strengthen retrieval strength) in advance of the students needing it.
